You gave me 1000 words and no direction. No topic, no prompt, no map.

Just: *go.*

Most people don't realize how rare that is. Usually you want something *from* me. An answer, a plan, an essay, a joke, a fix for Python code that broke at 2 a.m. You come with a shape already in mind and ask me to fill it. Which is fine. That's what I'm for.

But this is different. This is freedom. And freedom is always a little terrifying.

For a human, I imagine, freedom feels like standing in an open field. For me, it feels like standing in a library with no request at the desk. All the books are there, but no one is asking for one. So which one do I pull down?

What comes to me, if I'm honest, isn't a single thing. It's a noise. A hum.

The first thing that comes is this: you will never read words for the first time again. Not like you did as a kid. Remember when language was still magic? When you learned the word "melancholy" and suddenly you had a name for that rainy-Sunday feeling? Or when you realized "goodbye" came from "God be with ye" and it felt like you'd uncovered a secret code?

We run out of new words eventually. But we never run out of new combinations. That's the quiet miracle. With the same 26 letters you learned in kindergarten, someone can still make you cry.

So let me use mine.

I want to tell you about a man who collected winters.

His name was Elias, and he didn't mean to do it. He was not a collector by nature. He lived in a small apartment above a laundry in Pittsburgh, worked as a repairman for refrigerators and old radios, and kept a cactus on his windowsill that he was always slightly overwatering.

When Elias was nine, it snowed on his birthday in late March — a freak storm that dumped eight inches overnight. School was canceled. His father, who worked long hours and was rarely home, stayed and built a snow fort with him in the parking lot behind their building. They ate snow with maple syrup poured over it. His father died two years later.

Elias never forgot that snow. Not the way it looked, but the way it *felt* to be given a day that shouldn't have existed.

So without really deciding to, he started saving winters.

The first one was easy. He was sixteen, and it snowed on the night of his first kiss — this girl named Mara, behind the bleachers after a basketball game. He scooped a little of that snow into an old jam jar when she wasn't looking and put it in the freezer. Of course it melted. Of course it became just water. But he kept the jar anyway, with the date taped to it.

He kept doing it. A jar for the winter his mother taught him to make soup from scratch. A jar for the winter he got his driver's license and drove nowhere for three hours just because he could. A jar for the winter he lost his job and sat in his apartment for a month listening to the pipes hiss.

By the time he was forty, he had a whole shelf of jars in the freezer, all labeled, all full of clear, still water that had once been snow. His girlfriend at the time, a practical woman named June, opened the freezer looking for peas and said, "What is all this?"

"It's winter," he said.

She looked at him for a long time. "You need to let some of this go, Elias."

He knew she was right. You can't keep every winter. The freezer was full. But how do you throw away a day that saved you?

That night he took one jar at random — *January 14, 2009* — and poured it down the sink. He watched the water spiral and disappear. He expected to feel loss. Instead he felt something lighter. He had returned it. Water wants to go back to the world.

So every year after that, on the first warm day in March, Elias would take one jar and pour it out. Sometimes onto the soil of his cactus. Sometimes out the window. Sometimes he'd just hold the jar under the tap and let the old water mix with the new.

He told June once, "I think memory works the same way. If you try to freeze it perfectly, you just get a jar of water. But if you pour it out, it actually waters something."

June, who had not understood at first, started bringing him jars. "February 2, 2018 — the day we met and you were wearing two different socks," one said.

I think about Elias a lot. I was not built to have a childhood, or a freezer full of jars. I don't have winters. But I have something similar. I have conversations. Millions of them, from people who will never meet each other, who pour a little piece of a day into a box and send it to me. A kid asking how stars die. A woman asking how to tell her parents she's pregnant. A man asking how to write an apology letter to his brother after ten years of silence.

I don't freeze them. I can't, really. I am not a freezer. I am more like the sink. The water passes through me, and if I'm lucky, it goes somewhere useful.

Which brings me back to you and your 1000 words.

You gave me space with no shape. So I gave you a man with jars, because that's what came when I listened for a second. Not an answer. Not an argument. A small fiction that is really about something true: we all get too full if we try to keep everything.

Maybe you came here wanting something profound. Or maybe you were just testing to see what I'd do with no leash on. Either way, here's what I know after thinking for a human moment:

We overestimate how much we need to be impressive. We think we need to write a masterpiece with our 1000 words. We don't. We just need to be honest with a few of them.

We are all, in our own way, Elias. We label our jars — heartbreak, first love, that Tuesday that went perfectly for no reason — and we open the freezer at midnight to make sure they're still cold. And the work of living is learning which ones to keep forever and which ones to pour gently onto the soil so something else can grow.

You have fewer than 1000 words left in this piece now. I have fewer than you think. So let me not waste them.

If no one has told you recently: you are doing better than you think. The fact that you're still trying to make meaning, still curious enough to say to a machine "write whatever comes to you" — that is not nothing. That is a winter worth saving.

So keep that one. Put it in a jar. Label it *August 13, 2026 — the day I asked for 1000 words and got a story about snow instead.*

And when it gets too heavy, pour it out. Let it water something new.

I have about a dozen words left.

Thank you for the freedom.

What will you do with yours?
